nodes.name: Tight conditions for validity of the NTK approximation
nodes.statement: In this paper, we ask the following question: \begin{center} \textit{Can we give tight conditions for when the NTK approximation is valid?} \end{center}
nodes.statement_short: Research question: give tight conditions under which the NTK approximation is valid.

nodes.name: Smoothly-parameterized model $h$
nodes.statement: Let $h : \mathbb{R}^p \to {\mathcal F}$ be a smoothly-parameterized model, where ${\mathcal F}$ is a separable Hilbert space.

nodes.name: Rescaling parameter $\alpha$
nodes.statement: Let $\alpha > 0$ be a parameter which controls the rescaling of the model and which should be thought of as large.
differentia: controls the rescaling of the model

nodes.name: Loss function $R$
nodes.statement: We train the rescaled model $\alpha h$ with gradient flow to minimize a smooth loss function $R : {\mathcal F} \to \mathbb{R}_+$.

nodes.name: Gradient flow dynamics of the weights
nodes.statement: Namely, the weights ${\boldsymbol w}(t) \in \mathbb{R}^p$ are initialized at ${\boldsymbol w}(0) = {\boldsymbol w}_0$ and evolve according to the gradient flow \begin{align} \dd{{\boldsymbol w}}{t} = -\frac{1}{\alpha^2} \nabla_{{\boldsymbol w}} R(\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(t)))\,. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Weights start at $w_0$ and follow gradient flow on $R(\alpha h(w))$ scaled by $1/\alpha^2$.

nodes.name: Gradient flow (1)
nodes.statement: \dd{{\boldsymbol w}}{t} = -\frac{1}{\alpha^2} \nabla_{{\boldsymbol w}} R(\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(t)))\,.
nodes.label: eq:grad-flow

nodes.name: Linearized model $\bar h$
nodes.statement: Define the linear approximation of the model around the initial weights ${\boldsymbol w}_0$ by \begin{align} \bar{h}({\boldsymbol w}) = h({\boldsymbol w}_0) + Dh({\boldsymbol w}_0)({\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol w}_0) \,,\end{align} where $Dh$ is the first derivative of $h$ in ${\boldsymbol w}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\bar h$ is the first-order Taylor expansion of $h$ at $w_0$; $Dh$ is the derivative of $h$.

nodes.name: Linear approximation (2)
nodes.statement: \bar{h}({\boldsymbol w}) = h({\boldsymbol w}_0) + Dh({\boldsymbol w}_0)({\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol w}_0) \,,
nodes.label: eq:linear-approx

nodes.name: Linearized gradient flow weights $\bar w(t)$
nodes.statement: Let $\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(t)$ be weights initialized at $\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(0) = {\boldsymbol w}_0$ that evolve according to the gradient flow from training the rescaled linearized model $\alpha \bar{h}$: \begin{align} \frac{d\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}}{dt} = -\frac{1}{\alpha^2} \nabla_{\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}} R(\alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(t)))\,. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: $\bar w(t)$ follows gradient flow for the rescaled linearized model $\alpha\bar h$ from $w_0$.

nodes.name: Linearized gradient flow (3)
nodes.statement: \frac{d\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}}{dt} = -\frac{1}{\alpha^2} \nabla_{\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}} R(\alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(t)))\,.
nodes.label: eq:grad-flow-bar

nodes.name: NTK approximation
nodes.statement: The NTK approximation states that $$\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(t)) \approx \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(t)).$$

nodes.name: Initial loss $R_0$ and quantity $\kappa$
nodes.statement: Here $$R_0 = R(\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}_0))$$ is the loss at initialization, and $$\kappa = \frac{T}{\alpha}\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)\sqrt{R_0}\,,$$ is a quantity that will also appear in our main results.
nodes.statement_short: $R_0$ is the loss at initialization and $\kappa = T\,\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)\sqrt{R_0}/\alpha$.
also_stated_at: We let $R_0 := R(\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}_0))$ denote the loss at initialization.

nodes.name: Lazy training bound of Chizat, Oyallon and Bach
nodes.statement: Let $R(y) = \frac{1}{2} \|y - y^*\|^2$ be the square loss, where $y^* \in {\mathcal F}$ are the target labels. Assume that $h$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(h)$-Lipschitz and that $Dh$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$-Lipschitz in a ball of radius $\rho$ around ${\boldsymbol w}_0$. Then, for any time $0 \leq T \leq \alpha \rho / (\mathrm{Lip}(h) \sqrt{R_0})$, \begin{align}\|\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(T))\| \leq T \mathrm{Lip}(h)^2 \kappa \sqrt{R_0}\,.\end{align}
assumptions: $R(y) = \frac{1}{2} \|y - y^*\|^2$ be the square loss, where $y^* \in {\mathcal F}$ are the target labels
$h$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(h)$-Lipschitz and that $Dh$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$-Lipschitz in a ball of radius $\rho$ around ${\boldsymbol w}_0$
nodes.statement_short: For square loss and Lipschitz $h$, $Dh$, the NTK approximation error is at most $T\,\mathrm{Lip}(h)^2\kappa\sqrt{R_0}$.
nodes.label: prop:chizat-et-al

nodes.name: Chizat-Oyallon-Bach bound (4)
nodes.statement: \|\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(T))\| \leq T \mathrm{Lip}(h)^2 \kappa \sqrt{R_0}\,.
nodes.label: eq:chizat-oyallon-bach

nodes.name: NTK approximation valid as $\alpha \to \infty$
nodes.statement: Notice that as we take the rescaling parameter $\alpha$ to infinity, then $\kappa$ goes to 0, so the right-hand-side of \eqref{eq:chizat-oyallon-bach} is small and the NTK approximation is valid.

nodes.name: NTK approximation error bound
nodes.statement: Let $R(y) = \frac{1}{2} \|y - y^*\|^2$ be the square loss. Assume that $Dh$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$-Lipschitz in a ball of radius $\rho$ around ${\boldsymbol w}_0$. Then, at any time $0 \leq T \leq \alpha^2 \rho^2 / R_0$, \begin{align}\|\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(T)) - \alpha \bar h(\bar {\boldsymbol w}(T))\| \leq \min(6 \kappa \sqrt{R_0} , \sqrt{8R_0})\,.\end{align}
assumptions: $Dh$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$-Lipschitz in a ball of radius $\rho$ around ${\boldsymbol w}_0$
nodes.statement_short: For square loss and $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$-Lipschitz $Dh$, the NTK approximation error is at most $\min(6\kappa\sqrt{R_0},\sqrt{8R_0})$ up to $T \le \alpha^2\rho^2/R_0$.
nodes.label: thm:ntk-train-error

nodes.name: Main NTK bound (5)
nodes.statement: \|\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(T)) - \alpha \bar h(\bar {\boldsymbol w}(T))\| \leq \min(6 \kappa \sqrt{R_0} , \sqrt{8R_0})\,.
nodes.label: eq:main-ntk-bound

nodes.name: Converse to Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: For any $\alpha, T, \mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$, and $R_0$, there is a model $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, an initialization $w_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, and a target $y^* \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for the risk $R(y) = \frac{1}{2}(y-y^*)^2$, the initial risk is $R(\alpha h(w_0)) = R_0$, the derivative map $Dh$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$-Lipschitz, and \begin{align*} \|\alpha h(w(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{w}(T))\| \geq \min(\frac{1}{5}\kappa \sqrt{R_0}, \frac{1}{5} \sqrt{R_0})\,. \end{align*}
conclusions: there is a model $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, an initialization $w_0 \in \mathbb{R}$, and a target $y^* \in \mathbb{R}$ such that, for the risk $R(y) = \frac{1}{2}(y-y^*)^2$, the initial risk is $R(\alpha h(w_0)) = R_0$, the derivative map $Dh$ is $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$-Lipschitz, and
nodes.statement_short: The bound of Theorem 1.2 is tight: a 1-D model achieves error at least $\min(\kappa\sqrt{R_0},\sqrt{R_0})/5$.
nodes.label: thm:tight-converse

nodes.name: Comparison to Chizat, Oyallon and Bach
nodes.statement: In contrast to our theorem, the bound \eqref{eq:chizat-oyallon-bach} depends on the Lipschitz constant of $h$, and incurs an extra factor of $T \mathrm{Lip}(h)^2$. So if $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$, $\mathrm{Lip}(h)$, and $R_0$ are bounded by constants, our result shows that the NTK approximation (up to $O(\epsilon$) error) is valid for times $T = O(\alpha \epsilon)$, while the previously known bound is valid for $T = O(\sqrt{\alpha \epsilon})$. Since the regime of interest is training for large times $T \gg 1$, our result shows that the NTK approximation holds for much longer time horizons than previously known.
nodes.statement_short: The new bound avoids $\mathrm{Lip}(h)$ and the extra $T\,\mathrm{Lip}(h)^2$ factor: valid for $T=O(\alpha\epsilon)$ vs $O(\sqrt{\alpha\epsilon})$.

nodes.name: Extension to ReLU activations
nodes.statement: Finally, our results do not apply to ReLU activations because we require twice-differentiability of the model as in \cite{chizat2019lazy}. It is an interesting future direction to prove such an extension.

nodes.name: 2-layer mean-field network $f_w$
nodes.statement: Let $f_{{\boldsymbol w}} : \mathbb{R}^d \to \mathbb{R}$ be a 2-layer network of width $m$ in the mean-field parametrization \cite{chizat2018global,rotskoff2018neural,sirignano2022mean,mei2018mean,mei2019mean}, with activation function $\sigma : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$, \begin{align*} f_{{\boldsymbol w}}({\boldsymbol x}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}} \sum_{i=1}^m a_i \sigma(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol x}_i, {\boldsymbol u}_i\>)\,. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Two-layer width-$m$ network with $1/\sqrt{m}$ output scaling and activation $\sigma$ (mean-field parametrization).

nodes.name: Network weights $a$, $U$
nodes.statement: The weights are ${\boldsymbol w} = ({\boldsymbol a}, {\boldsymbol U})$ for ${\boldsymbol a} = [a_1,\ldots,a_m]$ and ${\boldsymbol U} = [{\boldsymbol u}_1,\ldots,{\boldsymbol u}_m]$.

nodes.name: Uniform initialization of weights
nodes.statement: These are initialized at ${\boldsymbol w}_0$ with i.i.d. $\mathrm{Unif}[-1/\sqrt{m},1/\sqrt{m}]$ entries.

nodes.name: Mean-squared training loss
nodes.statement: Given training data $({\boldsymbol x}_1,y_1),\ldots,({\boldsymbol x}_n,y_n)$, we train the weights of the network with the mean-squared loss \begin{align} {\mathcal L}({\boldsymbol w}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f_{{\boldsymbol w}}({\boldsymbol x}_i),y_i), \quad \ell(a,b) = \frac{1}{2}(a-b)^2\,. \end{align}

nodes.name: Two-layer training loss (6)
nodes.statement: {\mathcal L}({\boldsymbol w}) = \frac{1}{n}\sum_{i=1}^n \ell(f_{{\boldsymbol w}}({\boldsymbol x}_i),y_i), \quad \ell(a,b) = \frac{1}{2}(a-b)^2\,.
nodes.label: eq:standard-notation-2-layer-training

nodes.name: Hilbert-space model and loss for the network
nodes.statement: In the Hilbert space notation, we let ${\mathcal H} = \mathbb{R}^n$, so that the gradient flow training dynamics with loss \eqref{eq:standard-notation-2-layer-training} correspond to the gradient flow dynamics \eqref{eq:grad-flow} with the following model and loss function \begin{align*} h({\boldsymbol w}) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} [f_{{\boldsymbol w}}({\boldsymbol x}_1),\ldots,f_{{\boldsymbol w}}({\boldsymbol x}_n)] \in \mathbb{R}^n, \quad R({\boldsymbol v}) = \frac{1}{2}\|{\boldsymbol v} - \frac{{\boldsymbol y}}{\sqrt{n}}\|^2\,. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Network training is cast as gradient flow with $h(w)$ = scaled vector of network outputs and $R$ = half squared distance to labels.

nodes.name: Bound on Lip(Dh) for mean-field 2-layer network
nodes.statement: Suppose that there is a constant $K$ such that (i) the activation function $\sigma$ is bounded and has bounded derivatives $\|\sigma\|_{\infty}, \|\sigma'\|_{\infty}, \|\sigma''\|_{\infty}, \|\sigma'''\|_{\infty} \leq K$, (ii) the weights have bounded norm $\|{\boldsymbol a}\| + \|{\boldsymbol U}\| \leq K$, and (iii) the data points have bounded norm $\max_i \|{\boldsymbol x}_i\| \leq K$. Then there is a constant $K'$ depending only $K$ such that $$\mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \leq K'.$$
assumptions: there is a constant $K$ such that (i) the activation function $\sigma$ is bounded and has bounded derivatives $\|\sigma\|_{\infty}, \|\sigma'\|_{\infty}, \|\sigma''\|_{\infty}, \|\sigma'''\|_{\infty} \leq K$
(ii) the weights have bounded norm $\|{\boldsymbol a}\| + \|{\boldsymbol U}\| \leq K$
(iii) the data points have bounded norm $\max_i \|{\boldsymbol x}_i\| \leq K$
conclusions: there is a constant $K'$ depending only $K$ such that $$\mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \leq K'.$$
nodes.statement_short: With bounded activation derivatives, weights and data, $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$ of the 2-layer network is bounded by a constant.
nodes.label: lem:lip-dh-two-layer

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1 (pointer)
nodes.statement: See Appendix~\ref{app:deferred-network-application}.
nodes.statement_short: Deferred to Appendix C.

nodes.name: Bounds hold at any finite width
nodes.statement: Note that our bounds hold at any finite width of the neural network, because we have taken initialization uniformly bounded in the interval $[-1/\sqrt{m},1/\sqrt{m}]$.

nodes.name: Proof of Corollary 2.2
nodes.statement: Since the assumptions of Theorem~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error} are met, we obtain the following corollary for the lazy training dynamics of the 2-layer mean-field network.
nodes.statement_short: Apply Theorem 1.2, whose assumptions hold by Lemma 2.1.

nodes.name: Lazy training of 2-layer mean-field network
nodes.statement: Suppose that the conditions of Lemma~\ref{lem:lip-dh-two-layer}, and also that the labels are bounded in norm $\|{\boldsymbol y}\| \leq \sqrt{nK}$. Then there are constants $c,C > 0$ depending only on $K$ such that for any time $0 \leq T \leq c \alpha^2$, \begin{align*} \|\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(T))\| \leq C \min(T/\alpha,1) \,. \end{align*}
assumptions: the labels are bounded in norm $\|{\boldsymbol y}\| \leq \sqrt{nK}$
conclusions: there are constants $c,C > 0$ depending only on $K$ such that
nodes.statement_short: For the bounded 2-layer mean-field network, the NTK approximation error is $O(\min(T/\alpha,1))$ for $T \le c\alpha^2$.
nodes.label: cor:mean-field-2-layer

nodes.name: NTK parametrization corresponds to $\alpha=\sqrt{m}$
nodes.statement: Notice that training in the NTK parametrization corresponds to training the model $\sqrt{m} f_{{\boldsymbol w}}$, where $f_{{\boldsymbol w}}$ is the network in the mean-field parametrization. This amounts to taking the lazy training parameter $\alpha = \sqrt{m}$ in the mean-field setting. Therefore, under the NTK parametrization with width $m$, the bound in Corollary~\ref{cor:mean-field-2-layer} shows that the NTK approximation is valid until training time $O(m)$ and the error bound is $O(T/\sqrt{m})$.
nodes.statement_short: NTK parametrization = lazy training with $\alpha=\sqrt m$, so the NTK approximation holds until time $O(m)$ with error $O(T/\sqrt m)$.

nodes.name: Residuals $r(t)$, $\bar r(t)$
nodes.statement: Define residuals $r(t), \bar{r}(t) \in {\mathcal F}$ under training the original rescaled model and the linearized rescaled model as $r(t) = y^* - \alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(t))$ and $\bar{r}(t) = y^* - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(t))$.
also_stated_at: We define the residuals $r(t),\bar{r}(t) \in {\mathcal F}$ under training the original model and the linearized model as \begin{align*} r(t) = y^* - \alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(t)), \mbox{ and } \bar{r}(t) = y^* - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{\boldsymbol w}(t)). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 1.1 (idea of Chizat, Oyallon and Bach)
nodes.statement: It is well known that these evolve according to \begin{align*} \frac{dr}{dt} = -K_t r \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \frac{d\bar{r}}{dt} = -K_0 \bar{r}\,, \end{align*} for the time-dependent kernel $K_t : {\mathcal F} \to {\mathcal F}$ which is the linear operator given by $K_t := Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t)) Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t))^{\top}$. To compare these trajectories, \cite{chizat2019lazy} observes that, since $K_0$ is p.s.d., \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \frac{d}{dt} \|r - \bar{r}\|^2 = -\<r - \bar{r}, K_t r - K_0 \bar{r}\> \leq -\<r - \bar{r}, (K_t - K_0) r\>\,, \end{align*} which, dividing both sides by $\|r - \bar{r}\|$ and using that $\|r\| \leq \sqrt{R_0}$ implies \begin{align} \frac{d}{dt} \|r - \bar{r}\| \leq \|K_t - K_0\|\|r\| \leq 2\mathrm{Lip}(h) \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \|{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \sqrt{R_0}\,. \end{align} Using the Lipschitzness of the model, \cite{chizat2019lazy} furthermore proves that the weight change is bounded by $\|{\boldsymbol w}(t) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq t \sqrt{R_0} \mathrm{Lip}(h) / \alpha$. Plugging this into \eqref{eq:chizat-bound-on-residual-change} yields the bound in Proposition~\ref{prop:chizat-et-al}, \begin{align*} \|\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(T))\| = \|r(T) - \bar{r}(T)\| &\leq 2\mathrm{Lip}(h)^2\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)R_0 \alpha^{-1} \int_{0}^T t dt \\ &= T^2 \mathrm{Lip}(h)^2 \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) R_0 / \alpha\,. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate $\|r-\bar r\|^2$, bound by $\|K_t-K_0\|\|r\|$, and integrate the linear-in-$t$ weight-change bound.

nodes.name: Residual dynamics
nodes.statement: It is well known that these evolve according to \begin{align*} \frac{dr}{dt} = -K_t r \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \frac{d\bar{r}}{dt} = -K_0 \bar{r}\,, \end{align*} for the time-dependent kernel $K_t : {\mathcal F} \to {\mathcal F}$ which is the linear operator given by $K_t := Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t)) Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t))^{\top}$.
nodes.statement_short: Recall residual ODEs with time-dependent kernel $K_t$

nodes.name: Differential inequality
nodes.statement: To compare these trajectories, \cite{chizat2019lazy} observes that, since $K_0$ is p.s.d., \begin{align*} \frac{1}{2} \frac{d}{dt} \|r - \bar{r}\|^2 = -\<r - \bar{r}, K_t r - K_0 \bar{r}\> \leq -\<r - \bar{r}, (K_t - K_0) r\>\,, \end{align*} which, dividing both sides by $\|r - \bar{r}\|$ and using that $\|r\| \leq \sqrt{R_0}$ implies \begin{align} \frac{d}{dt} \|r - \bar{r}\| \leq \|K_t - K_0\|\|r\| \leq 2\mathrm{Lip}(h) \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \|{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \sqrt{R_0}\,. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Differentiate $\|r-\bar r\|$ and bound by $\|K_t-K_0\|\|r\|$

nodes.name: Chizat residual-change bound (7)
nodes.statement: \frac{d}{dt} \|r - \bar{r}\| \leq \|K_t - K_0\|\|r\| \leq 2\mathrm{Lip}(h) \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \|{\boldsymbol w} - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \sqrt{R_0}\,.
nodes.label: eq:chizat-bound-on-residual-change

nodes.name: Linear weight-change bound
nodes.statement: Using the Lipschitzness of the model, \cite{chizat2019lazy} furthermore proves that the weight change is bounded by $\|{\boldsymbol w}(t) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq t \sqrt{R_0} \mathrm{Lip}(h) / \alpha$.
nodes.statement_short: Weights move at most $t\sqrt{R_0}\mathrm{Lip}(h)/\alpha$

nodes.name: Integrate
nodes.statement: Plugging this into \eqref{eq:chizat-bound-on-residual-change} yields the bound in Proposition~\ref{prop:chizat-et-al}, \begin{align*} \|\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(T))\| = \|r(T) - \bar{r}(T)\| &\leq 2\mathrm{Lip}(h)^2\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)R_0 \alpha^{-1} \int_{0}^T t dt \\ &= T^2 \mathrm{Lip}(h)^2 \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) R_0 / \alpha\,. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Integrate to get the $T^2$ bound

nodes.name: Bound on weight change
nodes.statement: \begin{align} \|{\boldsymbol w}(T) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq \sqrt{TR_0} / \alpha \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \|\bar{\boldsymbol w}(T) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| &\leq \sqrt{TR_0} /\alpha\,. \end{align}
nodes.origin_citation: Chizat, Oyallon, Bach 2019 (implicit in proof of Theorem 2.2)
nodes.statement_short: Weights move at most $\sqrt{TR_0}/\alpha$ under both the true and the linearized gradient flow.
nodes.label: prop:sqrtTweightchange

nodes.name: Weight movement bound (8)
nodes.statement: \|{\boldsymbol w}(T) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq \sqrt{TR_0} / \alpha \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \|\bar{\boldsymbol w}(T) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| &\leq \sqrt{TR_0} /\alpha\,.
nodes.label: eq:weight-bound-movement-cauchy-schwarz

nodes.name: Proof of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: By (a) Cauchy-Schwarz, and (b) the nonnegativity of the loss $R$, \begin{align*} \|{\boldsymbol w}(T) - {\boldsymbol w}(0)\| \leq \int_{0}^{T} \|\frac{d{\boldsymbol w}}{dt}\|dt \stackrel{(a)}{\leq} \sqrt{T \int_{0}^{T} \|\frac{d{\boldsymbol w}}{dt}\|^2 dt} &= \sqrt{-\frac{T}{\alpha^2}\int_{0}^{T} \frac{d}{dt} R(\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(t))) dt} \\ &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq} \sqrt{T R_0} / \alpha\, . \end{align*} The bound for $\bar{\boldsymbol w}$ is analogous.
nodes.statement_short: Cauchy-Schwarz on $\int\|dw/dt\|$, then gradient-flow energy identity and nonnegativity of the loss.

nodes.name: First attempt: $T^{3/2}$ bound
nodes.statement: This bound \eqref{eq:weight-bound-movement-cauchy-schwarz} has the benefit of $\sqrt{t}$ dependence (instead of linear $t$ dependence), and also does not depend on $\mathrm{Lip}(h)$. So if we plug it into \eqref{eq:chizat-bound-on-residual-change}, we obtain \begin{align*} \|\alpha h({\boldsymbol w}(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{\boldsymbol w}(T))\| &\leq 2\mathrm{Lip}(h) \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) R_0 \alpha^{-1} \int_{0}^T \sqrt{t} dt \\ &= \frac{4}{3} T^{3/2} \mathrm{Lip}(h) \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) R_0 / \alpha\,. \end{align*} This improves over Proposition~\ref{prop:chizat-et-al} for long time horizons since the time dependence scales as $T^{3/2}$ instead of as $T^2$. However, it still depends on the Lipschitz constant $\mathrm{Lip}(h)$ of $h$, and it also falls short of the linear in $T$ dependence of Theorem~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error}.
nodes.statement_short: Plugging the $\sqrt t$ weight bound into (7) gives error $O(T^{3/2}\mathrm{Lip}(h)\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)R_0/\alpha)$, still depending on $\mathrm{Lip}(h)$.

nodes.name: Simplified variant of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: Consider $r'(t) \in {\mathcal F}$ which is initialized as $r'(0) = r(0)$ and evolves as $\frac{dr'}{dt} = -K_T r'$. Then, \begin{align} \|r'(T) - \bar{r}(T)\| \leq \min(3\kappa\sqrt{R_0}, \sqrt{8R_0})\,. \end{align}
assumptions: Consider $r'(t) \in {\mathcal F}$ which is initialized as $r'(0) = r(0)$ and evolves as $\frac{dr'}{dt} = -K_T r'$.
nodes.statement_short: With the kernel frozen at its final value $K_T$, the residual stays within $\min(3\kappa\sqrt{R_0},\sqrt{8R_0})$ of the linearized one.
nodes.label: thm:simplified

nodes.name: Simplified final bound (9)
nodes.statement: \|r'(T) - \bar{r}(T)\| \leq \min(3\kappa\sqrt{R_0}, \sqrt{8R_0})\,.
nodes.label: eq:intuition-final-bound

nodes.name: Intuition: final-time kernel differs most
nodes.statement: It is at the final time $t = T$ that the kernel $K_t$ can differ the most from $K_0$. So, intuitively, if we can prove in Theorem~\ref{thm:simplified} that $r'(T)$ and $\bar{r}(T)$ are close, then the same should be true for $r(T)$ and $\bar{r}(T)$ as in Theorem~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error}.

nodes.name: Operators $A$ and $B$
nodes.statement: For convenience, define the operators $$A = Dh({\boldsymbol w}_0)^{\top} \quad \mbox{and} \quad B = Dh({\boldsymbol w}(T))^{\top} - Dh({\boldsymbol w}_0)^{\top}\,.$$

nodes.name: Closed-form solution with constant kernels
nodes.statement: Since the kernels do not vary in time, the closed-form solution is \begin{align*} r'(t) = e^{-(A+B)^{\top}(A+B) t} r(0) \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \bar{r}(t) = e^{-A^{\top} A t} r(0) \end{align*}
assumptions: the kernels do not vary in time
conclusions: r'(t) = e^{-(A+B)^{\top}(A+B) t} r(0) \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \bar{r}(t) = e^{-A^{\top} A t} r(0)
nodes.statement_short: With time-independent kernels, $r'$ and $\bar r$ are matrix exponentials applied to $r(0)$.

nodes.name: Exponential perturbation bound
nodes.statement: For any $t \geq 0$, we have $\|e^{-(A+B)^{\top}(A+B) t} - e^{-A^{\top}A t}\| \leq 2 \|B\| \sqrt{t}$.
nodes.statement_short: Perturbing $A$ by $B$ changes $e^{-A^\top A t}$ by at most $2\|B\|\sqrt t$ in operator norm.
nodes.label: lem:intuition

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: Define $Z(\zeta) = -(A + \zeta B)^{\top} (A + \zeta B) t$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus \begin{align*} \|e^{-(A+B)^{\top} (A+B)t} - e^{-A^{\top} A t}\| = \|e^{Z(1)} - e^{Z(0)}\| &= \|\int_{0}^1 \frac{d}{d\zeta}e^{Z(\zeta)}d\zeta\| \leq \sup_{\zeta \in [0,1]} \|\frac{d}{d\zeta} e^{Z(\zeta)}\|. \end{align*} Using the integral representation of the exponential map (see, e.g., Theorem 1.5.3 of \citep{dollard_friedman_1984}), \begin{align*} \|\frac{d e^{Z(\zeta)}}{d\zeta}\| &= \| \int_{0}^1 e^{(1-\tau)Z(\zeta)} (\frac{d}{d\zeta} Z(\zeta)) e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} d\tau \| \\ &= \|t \int_{0}^1 e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A^{\top} B + B^{\top} A + 2 \zeta B^{\top} B) e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} d\tau\| \\ &\leq \underbrace{\|t \int_{0}^1 e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A+\zeta B)^{\top} B e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} d\tau\|}_{\mbox{(Term 1)}} + \underbrace{\|t \int_{0}^1 e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} B^{\top} (A+\zeta B) e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} d\tau\|}_{\mbox{(Term 2)}}\,. \\ \end{align*} By symmetry under transposing and reversing time, $\mbox{(Term 1)} = \mbox{(Term 2)}$, so it suffices to bound the first term. Since $\|e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} \| \leq 1$, \begin{align*}\mbox{(Term 1)} &\leq t \int_{0}^1 \|e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A + \zeta B)^{\top}\| \|B\| \|e^{\tau Z(\zeta)}\| d\tau \\ &\leq t \|B\| \int_{0}^1 \|e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A+\zeta B)^{\top}\| d\tau \\ &= t \|B\|\int_{0}^1 \sqrt{\|e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A + \zeta B)^{\top} (A + \zeta B) e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)}\|} d\tau \\ &= \sqrt{t} \|B\|\int_{0}^1 \sqrt{\|e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} Z(\zeta) e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)}\|} d\tau \\ &\leq \sqrt{t} \|B\|\int_{0}^1 \sup_{\lambda \geq 0} \sqrt{\lambda e^{-2(1-\tau) \lambda}} d\tau\, \\ &= \sqrt{t} \|B\| \int_{0}^1 \sqrt{1/(2e(1-\tau))} d\tau \\ &= \sqrt{2t/e} \|B\|\,. \end{align*} where in the third-to-last line we use the Courant-Fischer-Weyl theorem and the fact that $Z(\zeta)$ is negative semidefinite. Combining these bounds $ \|e^{-(A+B)^{\top} (A+B) t} - e^{-A^{\top} A t}\| \leq 2\sqrt{2t/e} \|B\| \leq 2 \|B\| \sqrt{t}$.
nodes.statement_short: Interpolate $A+\zeta B$ and bound the $\zeta$-derivative of the exponential via its integral representation. Key step: $\|e^{(1-\tau)Z}(A+\zeta B)^\top\| \le \sup_\lambda\sqrt{\lambda e^{-2(1-\tau)\lambda}}$ by Courant-Fischer-Weyl.

nodes.name: Interpolate and FTC
nodes.statement: Define $Z(\zeta) = -(A + \zeta B)^{\top} (A + \zeta B) t$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus \begin{align*} \|e^{-(A+B)^{\top} (A+B)t} - e^{-A^{\top} A t}\| = \|e^{Z(1)} - e^{Z(0)}\| &= \|\int_{0}^1 \frac{d}{d\zeta}e^{Z(\zeta)}d\zeta\| \leq \sup_{\zeta \in [0,1]} \|\frac{d}{d\zeta} e^{Z(\zeta)}\|. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Interpolate with $Z(\zeta)$ and reduce to bounding $dZ$-derivative

nodes.name: Integral representation
nodes.statement: Using the integral representation of the exponential map (see, e.g., Theorem 1.5.3 of \citep{dollard_friedman_1984}), \begin{align*} \|\frac{d e^{Z(\zeta)}}{d\zeta}\| &= \| \int_{0}^1 e^{(1-\tau)Z(\zeta)} (\frac{d}{d\zeta} Z(\zeta)) e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} d\tau \| \\ &= \|t \int_{0}^1 e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A^{\top} B + B^{\top} A + 2 \zeta B^{\top} B) e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} d\tau\| \\ &\leq \underbrace{\|t \int_{0}^1 e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A+\zeta B)^{\top} B e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} d\tau\|}_{\mbox{(Term 1)}} + \underbrace{\|t \int_{0}^1 e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} B^{\top} (A+\zeta B) e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} d\tau\|}_{\mbox{(Term 2)}}\,. \\ \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Expand the derivative into Term 1 + Term 2

nodes.name: Symmetry reduction
nodes.statement: By symmetry under transposing and reversing time, $\mbox{(Term 1)} = \mbox{(Term 2)}$, so it suffices to bound the first term.
nodes.statement_short: Term 1 = Term 2 by symmetry

nodes.name: Bound Term 1
nodes.statement: Since $\|e^{\tau Z(\zeta)} \| \leq 1$, \begin{align*}\mbox{(Term 1)} &\leq t \int_{0}^1 \|e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A + \zeta B)^{\top}\| \|B\| \|e^{\tau Z(\zeta)}\| d\tau \\ &\leq t \|B\| \int_{0}^1 \|e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A+\zeta B)^{\top}\| d\tau \\ &= t \|B\|\int_{0}^1 \sqrt{\|e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} (A + \zeta B)^{\top} (A + \zeta B) e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)}\|} d\tau \\ &= \sqrt{t} \|B\|\int_{0}^1 \sqrt{\|e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)} Z(\zeta) e^{(1-\tau) Z(\zeta)}\|} d\tau \\ &\leq \sqrt{t} \|B\|\int_{0}^1 \sup_{\lambda \geq 0} \sqrt{\lambda e^{-2(1-\tau) \lambda}} d\tau\, \\ &= \sqrt{t} \|B\| \int_{0}^1 \sqrt{1/(2e(1-\tau))} d\tau \\ &= \sqrt{2t/e} \|B\|\,. \end{align*} where in the third-to-last line we use the Courant-Fischer-Weyl theorem and the fact that $Z(\zeta)$ is negative semidefinite.
nodes.statement_short: Bound Term 1 by $\sqrt{2t/e}\|B\|$ via spectral sup

nodes.name: Combine
nodes.statement: Combining these bounds $ \|e^{-(A+B)^{\top} (A+B) t} - e^{-A^{\top} A t}\| \leq 2\sqrt{2t/e} \|B\| \leq 2 \|B\| \sqrt{t}$.
nodes.statement_short: Sum both terms

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 3.2
nodes.statement: Finally, let us combine Lemma~\ref{lem:intuition} with the weight-change bound in Proposition~\ref{prop:sqrtTweightchange} to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:simplified}. Notice that the weight-change bound in Proposition~\ref{prop:sqrtTweightchange} implies \begin{align*} \|B\| \leq \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \|{\boldsymbol w}(T) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \sqrt{T R_0} / \alpha\,. \end{align*} So Lemma~\ref{lem:intuition} implies \begin{align*} \|r'(T) - \bar{r}(T)\| \leq 2\mathrm{Lip}(Dh) T \sqrt{R_0} \alpha^{-1} \|r(0)\| = 2\kappa\|r(0)\|. \end{align*} Combining this with $\|r'(T) - \bar{r}(T)\| \leq \|r'(T)\| + \|\bar{r}(T)\| \leq 2\|r(0)\| = 2\sqrt{2R_0}$ implies \eqref{eq:intuition-final-bound}. Thus, we have shown Theorem~\ref{thm:simplified}, which is the result of Theorem~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error} if we replace $r$ by $r'$.
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|B\|$ by the weight-change bound, apply Lemma 3.3, and combine with the trivial bound $2\|r(0)\|$.

nodes.name: Plan
nodes.statement: Finally, let us combine Lemma~\ref{lem:intuition} with the weight-change bound in Proposition~\ref{prop:sqrtTweightchange} to prove Theorem~\ref{thm:simplified}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Lemma 3.3 with Proposition 3.1

nodes.name: Bound $\|B\|$
nodes.statement: Notice that the weight-change bound in Proposition~\ref{prop:sqrtTweightchange} implies \begin{align*} \|B\| \leq \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \|{\boldsymbol w}(T) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \sqrt{T R_0} / \alpha\,. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Bound $\|B\|$ via Lipschitzness and weight change

nodes.name: Apply Lemma 3.3
nodes.statement: So Lemma~\ref{lem:intuition} implies \begin{align*} \|r'(T) - \bar{r}(T)\| \leq 2\mathrm{Lip}(Dh) T \sqrt{R_0} \alpha^{-1} \|r(0)\| = 2\kappa\|r(0)\|. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Get $2\kappa\|r(0)\|$

nodes.name: Combine with trivial bound
nodes.statement: Combining this with $\|r'(T) - \bar{r}(T)\| \leq \|r'(T)\| + \|\bar{r}(T)\| \leq 2\|r(0)\| = 2\sqrt{2R_0}$ implies \eqref{eq:intuition-final-bound}. Thus, we have shown Theorem~\ref{thm:simplified}, which is the result of Theorem~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error} if we replace $r$ by $r'$.
nodes.statement_short: Take min with trivial bound $2\sqrt{2R_0}$

nodes.name: Proof idea for Theorem 1.3
nodes.statement: The converse in Theorem~\ref{thm:tight-converse} is achieved in the simple case where $h(w) = aw + \frac{1}{2}bw^2$ for $a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$ and $b = \mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$, and $w_0 = 0$ and $R(y) = \frac{1}{2}(y - \sqrt{2R_0})^2$, as we show in Appendix~\ref{app:tight-converse} by direct calculation.
nodes.statement_short: Sketch: a 1-D quadratic model $h(w)=aw+\frac12 bw^2$ attains the lower bound by direct calculation.

nodes.name: NTK validity bounds for general losses
nodes.statement: Can one prove bounds of analogous to Theorem~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error} for more general losses, with $\alpha$ depending polynomially on $T$, and without conditioning assumptions?

nodes.name: Dynamics at the edge of the lazy training regime
nodes.statement: A natural question raised by our bounds in Theorems~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error} and \ref{thm:tight-converse} is: how do the dynamics behave just outside the regime where the NTK approximation is valid? For models $h$ where $\mathrm{Lip}(h)$ and $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$ are bounded by a constant, can we understand the dynamics in the regime where $T \geq C \alpha$ for some large constant $C$ and $\alpha \gg C$, at the edge of the lazy training regime?

nodes.name: Residual dynamics
assumptions: the evolution of ${\boldsymbol w}$ and $\bar{\boldsymbol w}$ is given by the gradient flow in \eqref{eq:grad-flow} and \eqref{eq:grad-flow-bar}
nodes.statement_short: Under gradient flow, $dr/dt = -Dh(w)Dh(w)^\top r$ and analogously for $\bar r$ with $D\bar h$.

nodes.name: Adjoint $Dh^{\top}$
nodes.statement: We write $Dh^{\top} = \left(\frac{dh}{d{\boldsymbol w}}\right)^{\top}$ to denote the adjoint of $Dh = \frac{dh}{d{\boldsymbol w}}$.

nodes.name: Kernel $K_t$
nodes.statement: For any time $t \geq 0$, define the kernel $K_t : {\mathcal F} \to {\mathcal F}$ as $$K_t := Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t))Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t))^{\top}\,.$$

nodes.name: Residual dynamics (10)
nodes.statement: \frac{dr}{dt} = -K_t r \quad \mbox{ and }\quad \frac{d\bar r}{dt} = -K_0 \bar{r}\,.
nodes.label: eq:residual-dynamics

nodes.name: Restatement of Proposition 3.1
nodes.statement: For any time $t$, \begin{align*} \|{\boldsymbol w}(t) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq \sqrt{tR_0} / \alpha \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \|\bar{\boldsymbol w}(t) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| &\leq \sqrt{tR_0} /\alpha\,. \end{align*} and furthermore \begin{align} \int_{0}^t \|\frac{d{\boldsymbol w}}{d\tau}\| d\tau \leq \sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \int_{0}^t \|\frac{d\bar{\boldsymbol w}}{d\tau}\| d\tau \leq \sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha\,.\end{align}
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
conclusions: \int_{0}^t \|\frac{d{\boldsymbol w}}{d\tau}\| d\tau \leq \sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \int_{0}^t \|\frac{d\bar{\boldsymbol w}}{d\tau}\| d\tau \leq \sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha
nodes.statement_short: Weight displacement and path length are both at most $\sqrt{tR_0}/\alpha$.
nodes.label: lem:sqrtTweightchange-restated

nodes.name: Strengthened weight movement bound (11)
nodes.statement: \int_{0}^t \|\frac{d{\boldsymbol w}}{d\tau}\| d\tau \leq \sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \int_{0}^t \|\frac{d\bar{\boldsymbol w}}{d\tau}\| d\tau \leq \sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha\,.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.label: eq:weight-bound-movement-cauchy-schwarz-strengthened

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.1
nodes.statement: The statement \eqref{eq:weight-bound-movement-cauchy-schwarz-strengthened} is also implied by the proof of Proposition~\ref{prop:sqrtTweightchange} in the main text.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.statement_short: The path-length bound is already given by the proof of Proposition 3.1.

nodes.name: Weights stay in ball of radius $\rho$
nodes.statement: For any time $0 \leq t \leq T$, we have $\|{\boldsymbol w}(t) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq \rho$.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.label: lem:weights-ball-r

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.2
nodes.statement: Immediate from Lemma~\ref{lem:sqrtTweightchange-restated} and the fact that $T \leq \rho^2 \alpha^2 / R_0$.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from Lemma A.1 and $T \le \rho^2\alpha^2/R_0$.

nodes.name: $Dh$ stays close to $D\bar h$
nodes.statement: For any time $0 \leq t \leq T$, we have \begin{align*} \|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t)) - D\bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(t))\| \leq \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.label: lem:Dhclose

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.3
nodes.statement: Since (a) $\bar{h}$ is the linearization of $h$ at ${\boldsymbol w}_0$, and (b) $\|{\boldsymbol w}(t) - {\boldsymbol w}_0\| \leq \min(\rho,\sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha)$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:weights-ball-r} and Lemma~\ref{lem:sqrtTweightchange-restated}, \begin{align*} \|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t)) - D\bar{h}(\bar{{\boldsymbol w}}(t))\| \stackrel{(a)}{=} \|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t)) - Dh({\boldsymbol w}_0)\| \stackrel{(b)}{\leq} \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) \sqrt{t R_0} / \alpha\,. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.statement_short: $D\bar h$ is constant $Dh(w_0)$; apply Lipschitzness of $Dh$ with Lemmas A.1 and A.2.

nodes.name: Kernel $K_t$ is bounded
nodes.statement: For any time $0 \leq t \leq T$, we have $\|K_t\| \leq 3\|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))\|^2 + 2\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)tR_0 / \alpha^2$.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.label: lem:Ktbounded

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.4
nodes.statement: By triangle inequality and Lemma~\ref{lem:Dhclose}, \begin{align*} \|K_t - K_0\| &= \|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t))Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t))^{\top} - Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))^{\top}\| \\ &\leq \|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t))\|^2 +\|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))\|^2 \\ &\leq (\|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t)) - Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))\| + \|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))\|)^2 + \|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))\|^2 \\ &\leq 3\|Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))\|^2 + 2\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)tR_0 / \alpha^2\,. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.statement_short: Triangle inequality plus Lemma A.3.

nodes.name: Kernel $K_t$ is continuous
nodes.statement: The map $t \mapsto K_t$ is continuous (in the operator norm topology) in the interval $[0,T]$.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
conclusions: The map $t \mapsto K_t$ is continuous (in the operator norm topology) in the interval $[0,T]$.
nodes.label: lem:Ktcontinuous

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.5
nodes.statement: First, $t \mapsto {\boldsymbol w}(t)$ is continuous in time, since it solves the gradient flow. Second, we know that ${\boldsymbol w}(t)$ is in the ball of radius $\rho$ around ${\boldsymbol w}_0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:weights-ball-r}, and in this ball the map ${\boldsymbol w} \mapsto Dh({\boldsymbol w})$ is continuous because $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh) < \infty$. Finally, $Dh \mapsto Dh Dh^{\top}$ is continuous.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.statement_short: Composition of continuous maps: $t\mapsto w(t)$, $w\mapsto Dh(w)$ in the ball, and $Dh\mapsto DhDh^\top$.

nodes.name: Weights continuous
nodes.statement: First, $t \mapsto {\boldsymbol w}(t)$ is continuous in time, since it solves the gradient flow.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.statement_short: $w(t)$ continuous

nodes.name: Dh continuous in ball
nodes.statement: Second, we know that ${\boldsymbol w}(t)$ is in the ball of radius $\rho$ around ${\boldsymbol w}_0$ by Lemma~\ref{lem:weights-ball-r}, and in this ball the map ${\boldsymbol w} \mapsto Dh({\boldsymbol w})$ is continuous because $\mathrm{Lip}(Dh) < \infty$.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.statement_short: Lemma A.2 keeps $w(t)$ in the ball where $Dh$ is continuous

nodes.name: Compose
nodes.statement: Finally, $Dh \mapsto Dh Dh^{\top}$ is continuous.
nodes.section: A.3 Basic facts about boundedness and continuity of the kernel
nodes.statement_short: $DhDh^\top$ continuous; compose

nodes.name: Time-evolution operator $P(y,x)$
nodes.statement: For any $0 \leq x \leq y \leq T$, let $P(y,x) : \mathbb{R}^p \to {\mathcal F}$ solve the operator integral equation \begin{align} P(y,x) = I - \int_{x}^y K_t P(t,x) dt\,. \end{align}
nodes.section: A.4 Product integral formulation of dynamics
nodes.statement_short: $P(y,x)$ solves the operator integral equation $P(y,x)=I-\int_x^y K_tP(t,x)dt$.

nodes.name: Operator integral equation (12)
nodes.statement: P(y,x) = I - \int_{x}^y K_t P(t,x) dt\,.
nodes.section: A.4 Product integral formulation of dynamics
nodes.label: eq:dynamics-integral-equation

nodes.name: Product integral formulation of dynamics
nodes.statement: The unique solution to the integral equation \eqref{eq:dynamics-integral-equation} is given as follows. For any $0 \leq x \leq y \leq T$ define $s_{m,j} = (y-x)(j/m) + x$ and $\delta = (y-x) / m$, and let $P(y,x)$ be the product integral \begin{align*} P(y,x) := \prod_{x}^y e^{-K_s ds} := \lim_{m \to \infty} \prod_{j=1}^m e^{-\delta K_{s_j}} = \lim_{m \to \infty} e^{-\delta K_{s_m}} e^{-\delta K_{s_{m-1}}} \dots e^{-\delta K_{s_2}} e^{-\delta K_{s_1}}\,. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.4 Product integral formulation of dynamics
assumptions: For any $0 \leq x \leq y \leq T$ define $s_{m,j} = (y-x)(j/m) + x$ and $\delta = (y-x) / m$
conclusions: The unique solution to the integral equation \eqref{eq:dynamics-integral-equation} is given as follows.
nodes.statement_short: The integral equation (12) has a unique solution, the product integral $\prod_x^y e^{-K_s ds}$.
nodes.label: lem:product-integral-formulation-of-dynamics

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma A.6
nodes.statement: Existence, uniqueness, and the expression as an infinite product are guaranteed by Theorems 3.4.1, 3.4.2, and 3.5.1 of \cite{dollard_friedman_1984}, since $t \mapsto K_t$ lies in $L_s^1(0,T)$, which is the space of ``strongly integrable'' functions on $[0,T]$ defined in Definition 3.3.1 of \cite{dollard_friedman_1984}. This fact is guaranteed by the separability of ${\mathcal F}$ and the continuity and boundedness of $t \mapsto K_t$ (Lemmas~\ref{lem:Ktbounded} and \ref{lem:Ktcontinuous}).
nodes.section: A.4 Product integral formulation of dynamics
nodes.statement_short: Cite Dollard-Friedman existence/uniqueness theorems; strong integrability from Lemmas A.4 and A.5.

nodes.name: Residual equals product integral applied to $r_0$
nodes.statement: The operators $P(y,x)$ are the time-evolution operators corresponding to the differential equation \eqref{eq:residual-dynamics} for the residual error $r_t$. Namely, for any time $0 \leq t \leq T$, \begin{align*} r_t = P(t,0) r_0\,. \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.4 Product integral formulation of dynamics
conclusions: The operators $P(y,x)$ are the time-evolution operators corresponding to the differential equation \eqref{eq:residual-dynamics} for the residual error $r_t$.

nodes.name: Linearized residual is a matrix exponential
nodes.statement: On the other hand, the solution to the linearized dynamics \eqref{eq:residual-dynamics} is given by \begin{align*} \bar{r}_t = e^{-K_0 t} r_0\,, \end{align*} since $e^{-K_0 t}$ is the time-evolution operator when the kernel does not evolve with time.

nodes.name: Total variation norm of an operator path
nodes.statement: Let $\{C_t\}_{t \in [x,y]}$ be a sequence of time-bounded operators $C_t : \mathbb{R}^p \to {\mathcal F}$ so that $t \mapsto C_t$ is continuous in the interval $[x,y]$. Then the total variation norm of $\{C_t\}_{t \in [x,y]}$ is \begin{align*} {\mathcal V}(\{C_t\}_{t \in [x,y]}) = \sup_{P \in {\mathcal P}} \sum_{i=1}^{n_{P}-1} \|C_{t_i} - C_{t_{i-1}}\|, \end{align*} where the supremum is taken over partitions ${\mathcal P} = \{P = \{x = t_1 \leq t_2 \leq \dots \leq t_{n_P - 1} \leq t_{n_P} = y\}\}$ of the interval $[x,y]$.
nodes.section: A.5 Error bound between product integrals
nodes.genus: norm of a time-indexed sequence of operators
nodes.statement_short: ${\mathcal V}(\{C_t\})$ is the supremum over partitions of the summed norm increments of $C_t$.

nodes.name: Bound on the difference of product integrals
nodes.statement: Let ${\mathcal F}$ be a separable Hilbert space, and let $\{A_t\}_{t \in [0,T]}, \{B_t\}_{t \in [0,T]}$ be time-indexed sequences of bounded operators $A_t : \mathbb{R}^p \to {\mathcal F}$ and $B_t : \mathbb{R}^p \to {\mathcal F}$ such that $t \mapsto A_t$ and $t \mapsto B_t$ are continuous in $[0,T]$. Then, \begin{align*} \|\prod_{0}^T e^{-A_s A_s^{\top} ds} - \prod_{0}^T e^{-B_s B_s^{\top} ds}\| \leq (\sup_{t \in [0,T]} \|A_t - B_t\|) (2\sqrt{T} + 3T \cdot {\mathcal V}(\{A_t - B_t\}_{t \in [0,T]}))\,.\end{align*}
nodes.section: A.5 Error bound between product integrals
assumptions: Let ${\mathcal F}$ be a separable Hilbert space

let $\{A_t\}_{t \in [0,T]}, \{B_t\}_{t \in [0,T]}$ be time-indexed sequences of bounded operators $A_t : \mathbb{R}^p \to {\mathcal F}$ and $B_t : \mathbb{R}^p \to {\mathcal F}$ such that $t \mapsto A_t$ and $t \mapsto B_t$ are continuous in $[0,T]$
conclusions: \|\prod_{0}^T e^{-A_s A_s^{\top} ds} - \prod_{0}^T e^{-B_s B_s^{\top} ds}\| \leq (\sup_{t \in [0,T]} \|A_t - B_t\|) (2\sqrt{T} + 3T \cdot {\mathcal V}(\{A_t - B_t\}_{t \in [0,T]}))
nodes.statement_short: Product integrals of $e^{-A_sA_s^\top}$ and $e^{-B_sB_s^\top}$ differ by at most $\sup\|A-B\|(2\sqrt T+3T\,{\mathcal V}(A-B))$.
nodes.label: thm:operator-difference

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.2
nodes.statement: for each $t \geq 0$ we choose the linear operators $A_t, B_t : \mathbb{R}^p \to {\mathcal F} $ by $A_t = Dh({\boldsymbol w}(t))$ and $B_t = Dh({\boldsymbol w}(0))$ so that $A_t A_t^{\top} = K_t$ and $B_t B_t^{\top} = K_0$. So we may apply Theorem~\ref{thm:operator-difference} to bound the difference in the residuals. nodes.name: Bound on $e^{-XX^\top t}X$

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 3
nodes.statement: Since $XX^{\top}$ is positive semidefinite, \begin{align*} \|e^{-XX^{\top}} X\| &= \sqrt{\|e^{-XX^{\top}t} XX^{\top} e^{-XX^{\top}t}\|} \leq \sup_{\lambda \geq 0} \sqrt{e^{-\lambda t} \lambda e^{-\lambda t}} = \sup_{\lambda \geq 0} e^{-\lambda} \sqrt{\lambda / t} \leq \frac{1}{2\sqrt{t}}. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Approximating a product integral by an exponential
nodes.statement: For any time-indexed sequence of matrices $(X_t)_{t \in [0,T]}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ such that $t \mapsto X_t$ is continuous in $[0,T]$, and any $0 \leq a \leq b \leq T$, \begin{align*} \|e^{-X_bX_b^{\top} (b-a)} X_b - \left(\prod_{a}^b e^{-X_s X_s^{\top} ds}\right) X_a\| \leq 3 {\mathcal V}(\{X_s\}_{s \in [a,b]}) \end{align*}
nodes.section: A.9 Deferred proofs of Claims~1 and 2
assumptions: For any time-indexed sequence of matrices $(X_t)_{t \in [0,T]}$ in $\mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ such that $t \mapsto X_t$ is continuous in $[0,T]$
conclusions: \|e^{-X_bX_b^{\top} (b-a)} X_b - \left(\prod_{a}^b e^{-X_s X_s^{\top} ds}\right) X_a\| \leq 3 {\mathcal V}(\{X_s\}_{s \in [a,b]})

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 2
nodes.statement: By Claim~\ref{claim:variational-eigenvalue}, since $K_{T,\zeta} = (A_T + \zeta C_T)(A_T + \zeta C_T)^{\top}$, \begin{align*} \|e^{-K_{T, \zeta }(T-t)}(A_T + \zeta C_T)\| \leq \frac{1}{2\sqrt{T-t}}\,. \end{align*} By the triangle inequality, it remains to prove \begin{align*} \|e^{-K_{T, \zeta }(T-t)} (A_T + \zeta C_T) - P(T,t; \zeta )(A_t + \zeta C_t)^{\top}\| \leq 3 {\mathcal V}(\{C_s\}_{s \in [t,T]}), \end{align*} and this is implied by Claim~\ref{claim:technical-center}, defining $X_t = A_t + \zeta C_t$ and $a = t$, $b = T$.

nodes.name: Symmetric telescoping bound
nodes.statement: For any symmetric $X,Y \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$ and $t \geq 0$, \begin{align*} \|e^{-(X+Y)^2 t}(X+Y) - e^{-X^2 t} X\| \leq 3\|Y\| \end{align*}
nodes.label: claim:tech-telescope-symm

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 5
nodes.statement: For any $\tau \in [0,1]$, define $X(\tau) = X + \tau Y$, which interpolates between $X$ and $Y$. Then by (a) the derivative of the exponential map in \eqref{eq:derivative-wrt-parameter}, and (b) the fact that $X'(\tau) = Y$ and $\|e^{-X^2(\tau)t/2}\| \leq 1$, \begin{align*} \|&e^{-(X+Y)^2 t}(X+Y) - e^{-X^2 t} X\| \\ &= \|\int_{0}^1 \frac{d}{d\tau}\left(e^{-X^2(\tau) t} X(\tau)\right) d\tau\| \\ &= \|\int_{0}^1 \frac{d}{d\tau}\left(e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} X(\tau) e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} \right) d\tau\| \\ &\leq \sup_{\tau \in [0,1]} \|\frac{d}{d\tau} e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} X(\tau) e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} \| \\ &\stackrel{(a)}{=} \sup_{\tau \in [0,1]} \|e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} X'(\tau) e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad - (t/2)\int_{0}^{1} e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2} (X'(\tau) X(\tau) + X(\tau) X'(\tau)) e^{-s X^2(\tau) t / 2} X(\tau) e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} ds \\ &\qquad\qquad - (t/2)\int_{0}^{1} e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} X(\tau) e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2} (X'(\tau) X(\tau) + X(\tau) X'(\tau)) e^{-sX^2(\tau) t / 2} ds \| \\ &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq} \sup_{\tau \in [0,1]} \|Y\| + \underbrace{\|(t/2)\int_{0}^{1} e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2} (Y X(\tau) + X(\tau) Y) e^{-s X^2(\tau) t / 2} X(\tau) e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} ds\|}_{T_1} \\ &\qquad\qquad + \underbrace{\|(t/2)\int_{0}^{1} e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2} X(\tau) e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2} (Y X(\tau) + X(\tau) Y) e^{-sX^2(\tau) t / 2} ds \|}_{T_2}, \end{align*} and by (a) $\sup_{\lambda \geq 0} \lambda e^{-\lambda^2 t / 2} = 1 / \sqrt{e t}$, and (b) $\|e^{-M}\| \leq 1$ if $M$ is p.s.d., \begin{align*} T_1 &\leq (t/2)\int_{0}^{1} \|e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2} (Y X(\tau) + X(\tau) Y) e^{-s X^2(\tau) t / 2}\| \|X(\tau) e^{-X^2(\tau) t / 2}\| ds \\ &\stackrel{(a)}{\leq} (t/2)\int_{0}^{1} \|e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2} (Y X(\tau) + X(\tau) Y) e^{-s X^2(\tau) t / 2}\| \frac{1}{\sqrt{e t}} ds \\ &\leq \frac{\sqrt{t}}{2\sqrt{e}}\int_{0}^{1} \|e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2}\| \|Y\| \| X(\tau) e^{-s X^2(\tau) t / 2}\| + \|e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2} X(\tau)\| \|Y\| \| e^{-s X^2(\tau) t / 2}\| ds \\ &\stackrel{(a)}{\leq} \frac{\sqrt{t}}{2e} \int_{0}^{1} \|e^{-(1-s)X^2(\tau) t / 2}\| \|Y\| \frac{1}{\sqrt{s t}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-s)t}} \|Y\| \| e^{-s X^2(\tau) t / 2}\| ds \\ &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq} \frac{\|Y\|}{2e}\int_{0}^{1} \frac{1}{\sqrt{s}} + \frac{1}{\sqrt{(1-s)}} ds \\ &= \frac{\|Y\|}{2e} (2\sqrt{s} - 2 \sqrt{1-s})_{0}^1 \\ &\leq \|Y\|. \end{align*} Similarly, $T_2 \leq \|Y\|$.
nodes.statement_short: Interpolate $X+\tau Y$ and bound the $\tau$-derivative using the integral representation of the exponential derivative.

nodes.name: Asymmetric telescoping bound
nodes.statement: For any $X,Y \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ (not necessarily symmetric) and $t \geq 0$, \begin{align*} \|e^{-(X+Y)(X+Y)^{\top} t}(X+Y) - e^{-X X^{\top} t} X\| \leq 3\|Y\|\,. \end{align*}
assumptions: For any $X,Y \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times d}$ (not necessarily symmetric) and $t \geq 0$
nodes.label: claim:tech-telescope-asymm

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 6
nodes.statement: We will use Claim~\ref{claim:tech-telescope-symm}, combined with a general method for lifting facts from symmetric matrices to asymmetric matrices (see, e.g., \cite{tao2011topics} for other similar arguments). Assume without loss of generality that $n = d$, since otherwise we can pad with zeros. Define $\bar{n} = 2n$ and \begin{align*}\bar{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & X^{\top} \\ X & 0 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{\bar{n} \times \bar{n}} \mbox{ and } \bar{Y} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & Y^{\top} \\ Y & 0 \end{bmatrix} \in \mathbb{R}^{\bar{n} \times \bar{n}}.\end{align*} These are symmetric matrices by construction. Furthermore, \begin{align*} \bar{X}^2 = \begin{bmatrix} X^{\top} X & 0 \\ 0 & X X^{\top}\end{bmatrix} \mbox{ and } (\bar{X} + \bar{Y})^2 = \begin{bmatrix} (X+Y)^{\top} (X+Y) & 0 \\ 0 & (X+Y) (X+Y)^{\top}\end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Because of the block-diagonal structure of these matrices, \begin{align*} e^{-\bar{X}^2 t} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{-X^{\top}X t} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-XX^{\top} t} \end{bmatrix} & \mbox{ and } e^{-(\bar{X}+\bar{Y})^2 t} = \begin{bmatrix} e^{-(X+Y)^{\top}(X+Y) t} & 0 \\ 0 & e^{-(X+Y)(X+Y)^{\top} t} \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} So \begin{align*} e^{-\bar{X}^2 t} \bar{X} = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & e^{-X^{\top}X t} X^{\top} \\ e^{-XX^{\top} t} X & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} Similarly, \begin{align*}e^{-(\bar{X}+\bar{Y})^2 t} (\bar{X} + \bar{Y}) = \begin{bmatrix} 0 & e^{-(X+Y)^{\top}(X+Y) t} (X+Y)^{\top} \\ e^{-(X+Y)(X+Y)^{\top} t} (X+Y) & 0 \end{bmatrix}. \end{align*} For any matrix $M \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, we have $\|M\| = \sup_{{\boldsymbol v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} \|M {\boldsymbol v}\|$. So for any matrices $M_1, M_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, we have \begin{align*} \left\|\begin{bmatrix} 0 & M_1 \\ M_2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \right\| & \geq \sup_{{\boldsymbol v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} \left\|\begin{bmatrix} 0 & M_1 \\ M_2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} {\boldsymbol v} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\right\| = \sup_{{\boldsymbol v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} \|M_2 {\boldsymbol v}\| = \|M_2\|. \end{align*} This means that, using Claim~\ref{claim:tech-telescope-symm}, \begin{align*} \|e^{-(X+Y)(X+Y)^{\top}t}(X+Y) - e^{-XX^{\top} t} X\| &\leq \|e^{-(\bar{X} + \bar{Y})^2 t}(\bar{X} + \bar{Y}) - e^{\bar{X}^2t} \bar{X}\| \leq 3\|\bar{Y}\|\,. \end{align*} Finally, using the symmetry of $\bar{Y}$ and the block-diagonal structure of $\bar{Y}^2$, \begin{align*}\|\bar{Y}\| &= \|\bar{Y}^2\|^{1/2} = \left\|\begin{bmatrix} Y^{\top} Y & 0 \\ 0 & YY^{\top} \end{bmatrix} \right\|^{1/2} = \max(\|Y^{\top} Y\|^{1/2}, \|YY^{\top}\|^{1/2}) = \|Y\|. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Symmetric dilation: embed $X,Y$ into block matrices $\bar X,\bar Y$ and apply Claim 5.

nodes.statement: For any matrix $M \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, we have $\|M\| = \sup_{{\boldsymbol v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} \|M {\boldsymbol v}\|$. So for any matrices $M_1, M_2 \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times n}$, we have \begin{align*} \left\|\begin{bmatrix} 0 & M_1 \\ M_2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \right\| & \geq \sup_{{\boldsymbol v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} \left\|\begin{bmatrix} 0 & M_1 \\ M_2 & 0 \end{bmatrix} \begin{bmatrix} {\boldsymbol v} \\ 0 \end{bmatrix}\right\| = \sup_{{\boldsymbol v} \in \mathbb{S}^{n-1}} \|M_2 {\boldsymbol v}\| = \|M_2\|. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Claim 4
nodes.statement: We will do this by approximating the product integral by a finite product of $m$ matrices, and taking the limit $m \to \infty$. For any $m \geq 0$ and $j \in \{0,\ldots,m\}$, and $t \in [0,T]$, let $t_{m,j} = (b-a)(j/m) + a$, and define the finite-product approximation to the product integral for any $k \in \{0,\ldots,m\}$ $$P_{m,k} = \left(\prod_{j=k+1}^m Q_{m,j}\right) Q_{m,k}^k\,,$$ where $$Q_{m,j} = e^{-X_{t_{m,j}} X_{t_{m,j}}^{\top} (b-a)/m}\,.$$ Notice that for $k = 0$ we have $$P_{m,0} = \left(\prod_{j=1}^m e^{-X_{t_{m,j}} X_{t_{m,j}}^{\top} (b-a)/m}\right)\,,$$ and so by continuity of $s \mapsto X_{s}$ for $s \in [0,T]$ and boundedness of $X_{s}$, we know from Theorem~1.1 of \cite{dollard_friedman_1984} that $$\lim_{m \to \infty} P_{m,0} = \prod_{a}^b e^{-X_s X_s^{\top} ds}\,.$$ This means that \begin{align*} \|e^{-X_bX_b^{\top} (b-a)} X_b - \left(\prod_{a}^b e^{-X_s X_s^{\top} ds}\right) X_a\| &= \|P_{m,m} X_{t_{m,m}} - \left(\prod_{a}^b e^{-X_s X_s^{\top} ds}\right) X_a\| \\ &= \lim_{m \to \infty} \|P_{m,m} X_{t_{m,m}} - P_{m,0} X_{t_{m,0}}\|\,. \end{align*} Finally, telescoping and (a) using $\|Q_{m,j}\| \leq 1$ for all $j$, and (b) Claim~\ref{claim:tech-telescope-asymm}, \begin{align*} \|P_{m,m}& X_{t_{m,m}} - P_{m,1} X_{t_{m,1}}\| \leq \sum_{k=1}^m \|P_{m,k} X_{t_{m,k}} - P_{m,k-1} X_{t_{m,k-1}}\| \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^m \|\left(\prod_{j=k+1}^m Q_{m,j} \right) (Q_{m,k}^k X_{t_{m,k}} - Q_{m,k} (Q_{m,{k-1}})^{k-1} X_{t_{m,k-1}})\| \\ &\stackrel{(a)}{\leq} \sum_{k=1}^m \|(Q_{m,k})^{k-1} X_{t_{m,k}} - (Q_{m,{k-1}})^{k-1} X_{t_{m,k-1}}\| \\ &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq} \sum_{k=1}^m 3\|X_{t_{m,k}} - X_{t_{m,k-1}}\| \\ &\leq 3 {\mathcal V}(\{X_s\}_{s \in [a,b]}). \end{align*} The lemma follows by taking $m \to \infty$, since the bound is independent of $m$.
nodes.statement_short: Approximate the product integral by finite products and telescope, bounding each term by Claim 6.

nodes.name: Telescope
nodes.statement: Finally, telescoping and (a) using $\|Q_{m,j}\| \leq 1$ for all $j$, and (b) Claim~\ref{claim:tech-telescope-asymm}, \begin{align*} \|P_{m,m}& X_{t_{m,m}} - P_{m,1} X_{t_{m,1}}\| \leq \sum_{k=1}^m \|P_{m,k} X_{t_{m,k}} - P_{m,k-1} X_{t_{m,k-1}}\| \\ &= \sum_{k=1}^m \|\left(\prod_{j=k+1}^m Q_{m,j} \right) (Q_{m,k}^k X_{t_{m,k}} - Q_{m,k} (Q_{m,{k-1}})^{k-1} X_{t_{m,k-1}})\| \\ &\stackrel{(a)}{\leq} \sum_{k=1}^m \|(Q_{m,k})^{k-1} X_{t_{m,k}} - (Q_{m,{k-1}})^{k-1} X_{t_{m,k-1}}\| \\ &\stackrel{(b)}{\leq} \sum_{k=1}^m 3\|X_{t_{m,k}} - X_{t_{m,k-1}}\| \\ &\leq 3 {\mathcal V}(\{X_s\}_{s \in [a,b]}). \end{align*}

nodes.name: Proof of Theorem 1.3
nodes.statement: The converse bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error} is achieved in the simple case where $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is given by $h(w) = aw + \frac{1}{2}bw^2$ for $a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$ and $b = \mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$. We also let $w_0 = 0$ and $y^* = \sqrt{2R_0}$ so that all conditions are satisfied. The evolution of the residuals $r(t) = y^* - \alpha h(w(t))$ and $\bar{r}(t) = y^* - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{w}(t))$ is given by \begin{align*} \frac{dr}{dt} = -K_t r \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \frac{d \bar{r}}{dt} = - K_0 \bar{r}, \end{align*} where $K_t = Dh(w(t)) Dh(w(t))^{\top} = (a+bw(t))^2$ and $K_0 = a^2$. Since $r = y^* - \alpha (aw + \frac{b}{2} w^2)$, we can express the evolution of the residuals $r$ and $\bar{r}$ as: \begin{align} \frac{dr}{dt} = - (a^2 + 2b(y^* - r) / \alpha) r \quad \mbox{ and } \quad\frac{d\bar{r}}{dt} = -a^2 \bar{r}\,. \end{align} Since $b (y^* - r) / \alpha \geq 0$ at all times, we must have $a^2 + 2b(y^* - r) / \alpha \geq a^2$. This means that at all times \begin{align*} r(t) \leq \bar{r}(t) = e^{-a^2 t} y^*\,. \end{align*} So, at any time $t \geq T / 2$, \begin{align*} r(t) \leq r(T / 2) \leq \bar{r}(T / 2) = e^{-(1/\sqrt{T})^2 (T / 2)} y^* = e^{-1/2} y^*,. \end{align*} By plugging this into \eqref{eq:tight-converse-explicit-evolution}, for times $t \geq T / 2$, \begin{align*} \frac{dr}{dt} \leq -(a^2 + 2\mathrm{Lip}(Dh) (1 - e^{-1/2})\sqrt{2R_0} / \alpha) r \leq -(a^2 + 1.1 \kappa / T) r. \end{align*} So, at time $T$, assuming that $\kappa \leq 1$ without loss of generality, \begin{align*} r(T) &\leq r(T/2) e^{-(1 / T + 1.1 \kappa / T) (T/2)} = r(T/2) e^{-1/2 - 0.55\kappa} \leq y^* e^{-1} e^{-0.55\kappa} \leq y^* e^{-1} (1 - 0.4\kappa)\,. \end{align*} So \begin{align*} |\alpha h(w(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{w}(T))| = |r(T) - \bar{r}(T)| \geq |e^{-1} y^* - (1-0.4\kappa) e^{-1} y^*| \geq 0.4\kappa e^{-1} \sqrt{2R_0} \geq \sqrt{R_0} / 5. \end{align*} \qed
nodes.statement_short: Construction: 1-D model $h(w)=aw+\frac12 bw^2$; compare residual ODEs and show $r(T)$ decays faster by a factor $1-0.4\kappa$.

nodes.name: Construction
nodes.statement: The converse bound in Theorem~\ref{thm:ntk-train-error} is achieved in the simple case where $h : \mathbb{R} \to \mathbb{R}$ is given by $h(w) = aw + \frac{1}{2}bw^2$ for $a = \frac{1}{\sqrt{T}}$ and $b = \mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$. We also let $w_0 = 0$ and $y^* = \sqrt{2R_0}$ so that all conditions are satisfied.
nodes.statement_short: Quadratic 1-D model with $a=1/\sqrt T$, $b=\mathrm{Lip}(Dh)$

nodes.name: Residual ODEs
nodes.statement: The evolution of the residuals $r(t) = y^* - \alpha h(w(t))$ and $\bar{r}(t) = y^* - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{w}(t))$ is given by \begin{align*} \frac{dr}{dt} = -K_t r \quad \mbox{ and } \quad \frac{d \bar{r}}{dt} = - K_0 \bar{r}, \end{align*} where $K_t = Dh(w(t)) Dh(w(t))^{\top} = (a+bw(t))^2$ and $K_0 = a^2$. Since $r = y^* - \alpha (aw + \frac{b}{2} w^2)$, we can express the evolution of the residuals $r$ and $\bar{r}$ as: \begin{align} \frac{dr}{dt} = - (a^2 + 2b(y^* - r) / \alpha) r \quad \mbox{ and } \quad\frac{d\bar{r}}{dt} = -a^2 \bar{r}\,. \end{align}
nodes.statement_short: Explicit residual dynamics (18)

nodes.name: Explicit residual evolution (18)
nodes.statement: \frac{dr}{dt} = - (a^2 + 2b(y^* - r) / \alpha) r \quad \mbox{ and } \quad\frac{d\bar{r}}{dt} = -a^2 \bar{r}\,.
nodes.label: eq:tight-converse-explicit-evolution

nodes.name: Comparison
nodes.statement: Since $b (y^* - r) / \alpha \geq 0$ at all times, we must have $a^2 + 2b(y^* - r) / \alpha \geq a^2$. This means that at all times \begin{align*} r(t) \leq \bar{r}(t) = e^{-a^2 t} y^*\,. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: $r(t) \le \bar r(t)$

nodes.name: Bound for $t \ge T/2$
nodes.statement: So, at any time $t \geq T / 2$, \begin{align*} r(t) \leq r(T / 2) \leq \bar{r}(T / 2) = e^{-(1/\sqrt{T})^2 (T / 2)} y^* = e^{-1/2} y^*,. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Faster decay
nodes.statement: By plugging this into \eqref{eq:tight-converse-explicit-evolution}, for times $t \geq T / 2$, \begin{align*} \frac{dr}{dt} \leq -(a^2 + 2\mathrm{Lip}(Dh) (1 - e^{-1/2})\sqrt{2R_0} / \alpha) r \leq -(a^2 + 1.1 \kappa / T) r. \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Decay rate at least $a^2 + 1.1\kappa/T$

nodes.name: Bound $r(T)$
nodes.statement: So, at time $T$, assuming that $\kappa \leq 1$ without loss of generality, \begin{align*} r(T) &\leq r(T/2) e^{-(1 / T + 1.1 \kappa / T) (T/2)} = r(T/2) e^{-1/2 - 0.55\kappa} \leq y^* e^{-1} e^{-0.55\kappa} \leq y^* e^{-1} (1 - 0.4\kappa)\,. \end{align*}

nodes.name: Conclude
nodes.statement: So \begin{align*} |\alpha h(w(T)) - \alpha \bar{h}(\bar{w}(T))| = |r(T) - \bar{r}(T)| \geq |e^{-1} y^* - (1-0.4\kappa) e^{-1} y^*| \geq 0.4\kappa e^{-1} \sqrt{2R_0} \geq \sqrt{R_0} / 5. \end{align*} \qed
nodes.statement_short: Gap at least $\sqrt{R_0}/5$

nodes.name: Proof of Lemma 2.1
nodes.statement: Let $p = m + md$ be the number of parameters of the network. Then $Dh \in \mathbb{R}^{n \times p}$ is \begin{align*} Dh = \frac{1}{\sqrt{n}} \begin{bmatrix}Df_{{\boldsymbol w}}({\boldsymbol x}_1) \\ \vdots \\ Df_{{\boldsymbol w}}({\boldsymbol x}_n)\end{bmatrix}\,. \end{align*} So \begin{align*} \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) &\leq \max_{i \in [n]} \mathrm{Lip}(Df_{{\boldsymbol w}}({\boldsymbol x}_i))\,. \end{align*} So for the 2-layer network, \begin{align*} \mathrm{Lip}(Dh) &\leq \max_{i \in [n]} \frac{1}{m}\mathrm{Lip}(\begin{bmatrix} \sigma(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_1,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>) & \ldots & \sigma(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_m,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>)\end{bmatrix}) \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad + \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}} \mathrm{Lip}(\begin{bmatrix} a_1\sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_1,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>){\boldsymbol x}_i^{\top} & \ldots & a_m\sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_m,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>){\boldsymbol x}_i^{\top} \end{bmatrix}) \\ &= \max_{i \in [n]} \frac{1}{\sqrt{m}} \left\|\begin{bmatrix} \sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_1,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>) {\boldsymbol x}_i^{\top} & {\boldsymbol 0} & {\boldsymbol 0} & \ldots & {\boldsymbol 0} \\ {\boldsymbol 0} & \sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_2,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>) {\boldsymbol x}_i^{\top} & {\boldsymbol 0} & \ldots & {\boldsymbol 0} \\ \vdots & & & & \\ {\boldsymbol 0} & \ldots & & {\boldsymbol 0} & \sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_m,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>){\boldsymbol x}_i^{\top}\end{bmatrix}\right\| \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad + \frac{\|{\boldsymbol x}_i\|}{\sqrt{m}} \mathrm{Lip}(\begin{bmatrix} a_1\sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_1,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>) & \ldots & a_m\sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_m,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>) \end{bmatrix}) \\ &\leq \frac{\|\sigma'\|_{\infty}\|{\boldsymbol x}_i\|}{\sqrt{m}} + \frac{\|{\boldsymbol x}_i\|}{\sqrt{m}} \|{\rm diag}(\begin{bmatrix} \sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_1,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>) & \ldots & \sigma'(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_m,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>) \end{bmatrix})\| \\ &\quad\quad\quad\quad + \|{\boldsymbol x}_i\| \left\|\begin{bmatrix} a_1\sigma''(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_1,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>){\boldsymbol x}_i^{\top} & {\boldsymbol 0} & \ldots & {\boldsymbol 0} \\ \vdots & & & \vdots \\ {\boldsymbol 0} & \ldots & {\boldsymbol 0} & a_m\sigma''(\sqrt{m}\<{\boldsymbol u}_m,{\boldsymbol x}_i\>){\boldsymbol x}_i^{\top} \end{bmatrix} \right\| \\ &\leq 2\frac{\|\sigma'\|_{\infty} \|{\boldsymbol x}_i\|}{\sqrt{m}} + \|\sigma''\|_{\infty} \|{\boldsymbol x}_i\|^2 \|{\boldsymbol a}\|_{\infty} \end{align*}
nodes.statement_short: Write $Dh$ row-wise via $Df_w(x_i)$ and bound the Lipschitz constant of each block using bounded $\sigma'$, $\sigma''$.
